# H200 GPU rental rates fell from around $7/hour to around $4/hour in three weeks. · 2026-06-04T00:00:00+00:00

H200 GPU rental rates fell from around $7/hour to around $4/hour in three weeks.

→ The reflex read is that AI demand is rolling over.
→ The structural read is something else.
→ Two explanations hold up. One does not.

What is real: the Blackwell generation (B200 and GB200) is ramping fast and displacing Hopper-class hardware. Hyperscalers and neoclouds are discounting older chips to keep utilisation up.

This is generational transition, not demand collapse.

What is also real: the physical buildout is lagging silicon.

Power, cooling, transformers, and data centre permits have not kept pace with the chip ramp. A meaningful amount of compute is sitting idle waiting for grid hookups, and that unused capacity is leaking into the spot market at a discount.
This is a bottleneck cycle, not a demand signal. Exactly the kind of dynamic the ΣDX Fund is built to track.

What is being misread:
→ A 35–40% move in a thin spot market over three weeks is not an index.
→ Enterprise contracts at major clouds remain locked at term rates.
→ You do not get a regime change from a short window of spot dislocation.

highlights:
I've been in the GPUaaS market for over four years, back when the A100 was still the hottest GPU in the industry.

A lot has changed since then. New companies have emerged, model sizes have exploded, and AI adoption has accelerated far beyond what most people expected.

But even after watching this market every day for the last four years, I can't remember another period quite like the one we're seeing right now.

Demand is absolutely surging.

H100 and H200 pricing has nearly doubled compared to just a few months ago. Demand for new B200 and GB300 deployments has gone through the roof, and securing capacity is becoming increasingly challenging across the industry.

The appetite for compute has never been stronger.

Which raises a few questions:

If demand is this intense today, what will the GPU market look like by the end of the year?

Will supply finally catch up with demand?

results.title: Analyze whether GPU/accelerator supply…
highlights:
Nvidia's H100/H200 supply has eased substantially by mid-2026, with prices dropping sharply and wider availability, while Blackwell (B200/B300/GB200) remains tighter with lead times stretching into mid-2026 in places. This reflects ramped production, shifts away from Hopper, and hyperscaler buildouts, though CoWoS advanced packaging and HBM memory supply chains continue to constrain the absolute latest silicon. [1] [2] [3]

- H100 cloud rental rates fell from peaks of ~$8/hour in early 2025 to $1.90–$3.50/hour (or lower in some cases) by early 2026, with further stabilization or declines reported later. [1] [2]
- H200 is now widely available; B200/Blackwell shows limited early availability with premiums and stretched lead times (e.g., into June/July 2026 for some deployments), though supply is increasing. [1] [3] [4]
- Nvidia has phased down Hopper production to prioritize Blackwell; on-demand capacity for various SKUs has been sold out in periods, with 1-year contract prices rising ~40% in some windows due to sustained demand. [3] [4]
- Packaging (CoWoS) and HBM remain chokepoints, but capacity expansions (e.g., TSMC ramps) are helping; 2025–2026 production estimates show millions of H100-equivalent chips annually from Nvidia alone. [5]

...

### Nvidia GPU Supply and Pricing Dynamics (Post-Dec 2025)

Nvidia has curtailed Hopper (H100/H200) production to prioritize Blackwell ramp-up, leaving net-new Hopper supply extremely limited. New cluster deployments remain booked through at least August 2026, with Blackwell lead times extending into June–July 2026. On-demand capacity is largely sold out, and one-year contract rental prices for H100 rose nearly 40% from October 2025 to March 2026 (e.g., from ~$1.70/hr to $2.35/hr in some indices). B200 availability is improving gradually via hyperscalers but remains tight overall. [1] [2]

Persistent upstream constraints include advanced packaging (CoWoS) and especially HBM memory. HBM3E prices rose ~20% for 2026 deliveries amid demand from Nvidia H200 and custom ASICs; AMD cited memory costs as a driver for planned ~10% GPU price increases in 2026. These factors have sustained or increased effective pricing pressure even as some older GPU spot rates showed volatility or modest declines in certain reports. [3]

results.title: The Real TCO of a GPU Cluster: Hardware, Power, Staff (2026) | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
- GPU hardware is 25-35% of 5-year TCO on a self-built cluster. Power, cooling, networking, staff, and maintenance make up the other 65-75% (Introl, April 2026; KAD, April 2026)
- A 100-GPU H100 cluster runs ~$3M in hardware but $8.6M over 5 years all-in. Gartner: 73% of enterprises underestimate AI infrastructure costs by failing to account for opex (Introl, April 2026)
- On-prem effective rate for an 8-GPU H100 node is ~$4.75/GPU/hr before networking and facility lease. Spheron's on-demand H100 is $2.90/hr (Spheron, April 2026)
- A 256-GPU B200 cluster owned and colocated in Texas costs ~$15.5M over 3 years with loan + opex, or ~$2.88/GPU/hr at 80% utilisation. Buying beats renting above ~70% utilisation (American Compute, March 2026)
- Hyperscaler "all-in" pricing isn't free either. Egress, storage, support tiers, and reserved-but-idle capacity stack 20-40% on top of the compute rate
- GPUaaS.com offers both short-term and long-term contracts at rates hyperscalers won't offer you. H100 from ~$2.50/GPU/hr, H200 from ~$3.00/GPU/hr, B200 and B300 from ~$4.50/GPU/hr, with flexible commitment terms

...

GPUaaS.com contract rates run from ~$2.50/GPU/hr for H100, ~$3.00/GPU/hr for H200, and ~$4.50/GPU/hr for B200 and B300. Owned hardware lands at ~$2.88/GPU/hr effective for a 256-GPU B200 cluster at 80% utilisation (American Compute, March 2026). The trade-off is risk: GPUaaS.com absorbs the facility, the staff, the cooling, the GPU obsolescence, and the cash flow timing. You get dedicated NVIDIA infrastructure on a contract length that matches your utilisation confidence, with short-term and long-term contracts.

highlights:
# NVIDIA H200 at $2.16/hr: The Most Affordable On-Demand H200 in the Market

Samuelakansolo

Jun 4, 2026

Let’s strike the chord of the string here. Ocean Network is a decentralised peer-to-peer compute layer, offering the NVIDIA H200 SXM5 GPU at an affordable rate of $2.16/hr. This pricing comes with no minimum commitment, no 8-GPU stacked bundle, and it offers an escrow payment model that only charges when the job is completed.

...

Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers H200 GPUs through its 8-GPU P5e instances, with pricing starting at around $5 per GPU per hour at the lowest available rate. Microsoft Azure’s ND H200 configurations can reach roughly $13 per GPU per hour in some regions. Google Cloud does provide cheaper spot pricing, but the downside is that workloads can suddenly terminate whenever capacity becomes limited. Other providers like RunPod and Jarvislabs have made single-GPU access more available, but their H200 pricing still sits around $3.59 and $3.80 per hour. On top of that, users still face the risk of failed jobs without guaranteed protection or compensation if workloads stop midway through execution.

To bridge this gap, a decentralised peer-to-peer compute layer called the Ocean Network has changed this discourse. The Ocean Network is built on top of the Ocean Protocol Foundation. Through their dashboard, “ oncompute.ai,” you can successfully rent a verified NVIDIA H200 SXM5 node at a staggering price of $2.16 per hour, which equates to $0.036 per unit per minute. So here we are; let’s talk about what Ocean Network’s benefits are, the problems they’ve solved, and why it should be the alternative in the market right now.

...

Ocean Network is a decentralized peer-to-peer compute platform built to convert idle or underutilized GPU hardware into accessible pay-per-use computing resources. The process is simple: node operators provide their hardware to the network, users choose the setup that fits their needs, submit containerized workloads, and receive the completed results afterward. Everything happens without the hassle of managing remote servers, setting up SSH connections, or navigating through complicated cloud provider dashboards, making the experience much more streamlined for developers and researchers.

Ocean Network was developed by the Ocean Protocol Foundation, one of the leading organizations in the decentralized data and compute sector. Over the years, Ocean Protocol has focused on building infrastructure for tokenized data sharing and privacy-preserving computation, helping lay the groundwork for decentralized AI and data ecosystems. Ocean Network serves as the practical compute layer that transforms this infrastructure into a real-world cloud alternative. In March 2026, the platform officially launched its Beta phase alongside a strategic partnership with Aethir, a major GPU infrastructure provider. This collaboration was designed to ensure stable hardware availability and reliable performance during the platform’s early growth stage, before the peer-to-peer node marketplace fully matures.

One amazing feature about the Beta launch is that the Ocean Network is offering $100 in complimentary compute credits, otherwise called Compy tokens, to its early adopters who access dashboard.oncompute.ai. This ensures that a developer can test H200 workloads, which include real inference runs, embedding pipelines, and fine-tuning experiences, without being committed to a financial fee. The Compy tokens cover an approximate 46 hours of H200 compute time at the standard $2.16/hr rate, which is enough runway to evaluate the platform effectively.

...

The verified H200 node currently listed on the dashboard is a good example of this transparency in practice. Based in Kyoto, Japan, within the East Region, the setup includes two NVIDIA H200 SXM5 GPUs per environment and is powered by an Intel Xeon Platinum 8460Y+ processor. The Xeon Platinum belongs to Intel’s 5th-generation Sapphire Rapids lineup, which is specifically designed for high-performance data center workloads. The system also comes with 440GB of RAM and 1TB of NVMe storage per environment, giving users a complete and detailed breakdown of the hardware instead of leaving important specifications unclear.

Ocean Network’s pricing is set at $0.036 USDC per unit per minute, which is approximated at $2.16 per hour per GPU. The duration for job completion ranges from a minimum of one minute to a maximum of 12 hours. The Ocean Node runs on Node v3.1.0 and has completed over 2,200 jobs, earning over $586 in provider revenue. The 5th-generation Intel Xeon Platinum 8460Y+ pairing deserves attention because CPU bottlenecks come with a hidden cost in GPU compute configurations. At 40 cores and 440GB of RAM, the system can withstand and handle substantial data processing pipelines, tokenisation, and CPU-side data loading in parallel with GPU execution.

...

The table below reflects publicly available on-demand pricing as of May 2026. For AWS and Azure, which only offer H200 access in 8-GPU node configurations, the per-GPU figures shown divide the total node cost by eight for a fair comparison — but it is worth being explicit that in practice, you cannot rent a single H200 GPU from either of those providers. The minimum purchase is a full node.

...

Ocean Network appears to be the only provider in this comparison that combines all four features, offering an affordable charge of $2.16/hr with no minimum GPU commitment, an escrow-protected payment model, and single-GPU access.

Today, an independent developer or small AI team can launch a verified H200 node for around $2.16 per hour, run workloads on demand, and only pay once the job has been completed successfully. This creates a far more flexible and affordable way to access enterprise-level AI infrastructure.
